kaabu-empire.s: The Kaabu Empire was a Mandinka state in present-day Guinea-Bissau, Senegal and The Gambia. It emerged in the thirteenth century as an outlying province of the Mali Empire and later became independent.

kabongo-luba.s: Kabongo Luba was one of the two states into which the Luba kingdom split after a succession civil war in the late nineteenth century. Its rival was Kasongo Luba.

kabuki.s: Kabuki is a form of Japanese theatre combining drama, music and dance, known for stylised acting and elaborate costumes. It developed in the early seventeenth century and flourished in the urban culture of Edo.

kabul.s: Kabul is a city in present-day Afghanistan, strategically placed on routes between Central Asia and India. Babur, the last Timurid prince expelled from Central Asia, took Kabul and used it as his base.

kaidu.s: Kaidu was a Mongol prince, a grandson of Ögedei, who dominated Central Asia from 1272 to 1301. Allied with Duwa of the Chagatai Khanate, he waged long wars against Kublai Khan and the Yuan Dynasty.

kaifeng.s: Kaifeng is a city in north-central China on the Yellow River plain. It was the capital of the Northern Song and one of the largest and most commercialised cities of its time.

kairouan.s: Kairouan is a city in present-day Tunisia, founded in the seventh century as an early Arab Muslim centre and a seat of religious learning. Around 1040 CE the Gudala chieftain Yahya ibn Ibrahim met the jurist Abu Imran al-Fasi there.

kaiser.s: Kaiser is the German word for emperor, derived from the Roman name Caesar. In the German Empire it was the title of the King of Prussia as German Emperor, first held by Wilhelm I from 1871.

kaiyuan-era.s: The Kaiyuan era was the reign period of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang Dynasty from 713 to 741. It is regarded by Chinese historians as the Tang's cultural and administrative high point.

kalala-ilunga.s: Kalala Ilunga is the figure credited in oral tradition with founding the Second Luba Dynasty around c. 1585.

kaleb.s: Kaleb was a king of Aksum who reigned c. 514–542 CE.

kalebs-yemen-campaign.s: Kaleb's Yemen campaign was the Aksumite military expedition to South Arabia in the sixth century CE under King Kaleb. It followed the persecution of Christians by the Himyarite king Dhu Nuwas and was undertaken in co-operation with the Byzantine Empire.

kalidasa.s: Kalidasa was a classical Sanskrit poet and dramatist, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the language. His works include the drama Abhijnanashakuntalam and the poem Meghaduta.

kalinga.s: Kalinga was an ancient region on the eastern coast of India, roughly corresponding to present-day Odisha. It was conquered by the Maurya emperor Ashoka in a bloody war.

kalinga-war.s: The Kalinga War was the Maurya Empire's conquest of Kalinga under Ashoka, dated on the site to 261 BCE. Ashoka's own edicts record the great loss of life it caused.

kamal-ud-din-behzad.s: Kamāl ud-Dīn Behzād, or Bihzad, was a Persian painter of the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, the most celebrated master of the Herat school. He worked under Timurid patronage at the court of Husayn Bayqara.

kamikaze.s: Kamikaze, meaning divine wind, is the Japanese name for the typhoons that destroyed the Mongol invasion fleets sent against Japan by the Yuan Dynasty in the late thirteenth century. The storms helped preserve Japanese independence.

kandahar.s: Kandahar is a city in southern Afghanistan, long contested between Iranian and Indian powers. Under the late Safavid Empire, its Sunni Ghilzai Afghans revolted under Mir Wais from 1704.

kandake.s: Kandake was the title of royal women, often queen mothers or ruling queens, in the kingdom of Kush. Several kandakes held significant political authority and some ruled in their own right.

kanem-bornu-empire.s: The Kanem–Bornu Empire was a long-lived state around Lake Chad, first centred in Kanem and later in Bornu. It was ruled for centuries by the Sayfawa dynasty and was among the earliest states in the region to adopt Islam.

kanesh.s: Kanesh, modern Kültepe in Turkey, was an ancient city in central Anatolia. In the early second millennium BCE it hosted the most important Assyrian merchant colony, or karum.

kangaba.s: Kangaba is a region on the upper Niger in present-day Mali, the original heartland of the Keita dynasty. As the Mali Empire declined, the Keita rulers lost their wider territories.

kangxi-emperor.s: The Kangxi Emperor was one of the longest-reigning rulers in Chinese history, governing the Qing Empire from 1661 to 1722. He suppressed the Revolt of the Three Feudatories and took Taiwan from the Zheng family in 1683.

kaniaga.s: Kaniaga was a region in the western Sahel that was home to the Sosso kingdom, once a vassal of Ghana. Around 1140 the Sosso began subjugating Wagadou, the heartland of Ghana.

kano.s: Kano is a city in northern Nigeria and one of the historic Hausa city-states. Under the Sokoto Caliphate it became the principal commercial centre, famous for its indigo-dyed textiles traded across the Sahara.

kansala.s: Kansala was the capital of the Kaabu Empire in present-day Guinea-Bissau. It was the seat of the Mandinka ruling elite.

kanta-and-balama.s: The kanta and balama were professional military commanders appointed by Askia Muhammad in the Songhai Empire. Each was responsible for a specific territorial zone.

kanun.s: Kanun was the body of secular law issued by Ottoman sultans, alongside Islamic sharia. Suleiman the Magnificent, known as Kanuni or the Lawgiver, systematised it in codes governing criminal justice, land tenure and taxation.

kara-koyunlu.s: The Kara Koyunlu, or Black Sheep Turkomans, were a Turkoman tribal confederation that ruled parts of eastern Anatolia, Azerbaijan, Iraq and western Iran in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. They were rivals of the Aq Qoyunlu.

kara-mustafa-pasha.s: Kara Mustafa Pasha was an Ottoman grand vizier of the late seventeenth century. He led the Ottoman siege of Vienna in 1683, which was broken by a relief army under Jan III Sobieski.

karakorum.s: Karakorum was the capital of the Mongol Empire in central Mongolia, established under Ögedei. It was the seat of the Great Khan.

kardar.s: A kardar was a revenue officer in the administration of the Sikh Empire. Kardars collected land revenue assessed according to cultivation type and yield, through local intermediaries.

karelia.s: Karelia is a region between the Gulf of Finland and the White Sea, divided today between Finland and Russia. Parts of it were held by Sweden in the seventeenth century.

karim-khan-zand.s: Karim Khan Zand was the founder of the Zand dynasty, who ruled most of Iran from Shiraz after the collapse of Afsharid power, and died in 1779. He declined the title of shah and styled himself Vakil, or regent.

karl-i.s: Karl I, or Charles I of Austria, was the last Emperor of Austria and King of Hungary, reigning from 1916 to 1918. He sought a separate peace during the First World War without success.

karluks.s: The Karluks were a Turkic people of Central Asia. In 744 CE, together with the Uyghurs and Basmyls, they seized the Gokturk centre at Ötüken and killed the last Gokturk khagan.

karnak.s: Karnak is a vast temple complex at Thebes, present-day Luxor, dedicated chiefly to the god Amun. It was greatly expanded during the Egyptian New Kingdom, including a major building programme under Hatshepsut, and functioned as a religious and economic centre.

karum.s: A karum was a trading colony or merchant quarter in the ancient Near East. The best-known is Karum Kanesh in Anatolia, the centre of an Assyrian merchant network.

karun-river.s: The Karun River is the largest river in Iran, flowing through Khuzestan into the Shatt al-Arab. Under Shapur I, the Band-e Kaisar dam was built across it near Shushtar, reportedly with the labour and engineering skills of Roman prisoners.

kasai.s: Kasai is a region in the south of the present-day Democratic Republic of the Congo, named after the Kasai River. Lunda expansion under rulers such as the Mwaant Yaav extended the empire north into Kasai.

kasbah-of-the-udayas.s: The Kasbah of the Udayas is a fortress at the mouth of the Bou Regreg river in Rabat, Morocco. It was built up by the Almohads in the twelfth century as part of their development of Rabat.

kashgaria.s: Kashgaria is a historical name for the western Tarim Basin, centred on the oasis city of Kashgar in present-day Xinjiang. It was part of the territories received by Chagatai Khan from the former Qara Khitai realm.

kashmir.s: Kashmir is a mountainous region in the north of the Indian subcontinent, famed for its shawls. Ranjit Singh conquered it for the Sikh Empire, and its revenues and trade were important to the empire.

kashta.s: Kashta was a king of Kush in the eighth century BCE who extended Kushite authority into Upper Egypt. His successor Piye completed the conquest of Egypt.

kasongo-luba.s: Kasongo Luba was one of the two states into which the Luba kingdom divided after a succession civil war in the late nineteenth century. It was named after the claimant Kasongo Nyembo.

kasongo-nyembo.s: Kasongo Nyembo was a claimant to the Luba throne after the death of Ilunga Kabale. His civil war with the rival claimant Kumwimbe Tshimbu split the kingdom into Kasongo Luba and Kabongo Luba.

kassite-dynasty.s: The Kassite dynasty ruled Babylonia for about four centuries after the fall of the First Dynasty of Babylon. It was overthrown around 1158 BCE by the Elamite kings Shutruk-Nahhunte and Kutir-Nahhunte, who carried off monuments such as the Code of Hammurabi to Susa.

kassites.s: The Kassites were a people, probably from the Zagros region, who took control of Babylonia after the Hittite sack of Babylon and ruled it for about four centuries. They adopted Babylonian culture and the cult of Marduk.

kataphraktoi.s: Kataphraktoi, or cataphracts, were heavily armoured cavalry in which both rider and often horse were protected by armour. They were a core element of Parthian and Sasanian armies.

katoikia.s: A katoikia was a Greek or Macedonian military colony in the Hellenistic kingdoms, in which settlers received land in return for military service. The Seleucids founded many such colonies alongside new cities across their domains.

kavad-ii.s: Kavad II was a Sasanian king who deposed and killed his father Khosrow II in 628 CE after the defeat by Heraclius. He made peace with the Byzantines but died within the same year.

kay-tribe.s: The Kayı tribe was a branch of the Oghuz Turks. Ottoman tradition holds that Osman I, the founder of the dynasty, belonged to the Kayı clan.

kazakhs.s: The Kazakhs are a Turkic people of the Central Asian steppe. Their lands were progressively absorbed by the Russian Empire during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

kazallu.s: Kazallu was an ancient city-state in Mesopotamia. According to the site, Babylon was taken from Kazallu around 1894 BCE by the Amorite chieftain Sumuabum, who declared independence and began walling the city.

kazembe.s: Kazembe was a kingdom in the Luapula valley in present-day Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, founded by Lunda chiefs. In the period of their greatest extent, Luba military expeditions extended southward towards Kazembe.

kebek-coin.s: The kebek was a standardised silver coin introduced by Kebek Khan of the Chagatai Khanate in the 1320s. It was so widely trusted that it became the basis of later currency in the region.

kebek-khan.s: Kebek Khan was a ruler of the Chagatai Khanate in the early fourteenth century. In the 1320s he introduced a currency reform with standardised silver coins and tried to establish a settled capital at Qarshi in present-day Uzbekistan.

kebra-nagast.s: The Kebra Nagast, or Glory of the Kings, is an Ethiopian text compiled in Ge'ez in the medieval period. It tells of the Queen of Sheba, King Solomon and their son Menelik I, and the bringing of the Ark of the Covenant to Ethiopia.

kediri-kingdom.s: The Kediri Kingdom was a Hindu-Buddhist state in eastern Java that flourished in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Its rise, followed by that of Singhasari and Majapahit, created a powerful rival centre in the region.

kedukan-bukit-inscription.s: The Kedukan Bukit inscription is a stone inscription dated 682 CE, found near Palembang in Sumatra. Written in Old Malay, it is the earliest surviving example of that language.

keira-dynasty.s: The Keira dynasty was the ruling dynasty of the Darfur Sultanate, founded in the seventeenth century by Sulayman Solong. It ruled until the defeat of Sultan Ibrahim in 1874.

keita-dynasty.s: The Keita dynasty was the ruling Mandinka lineage of the Mali Empire, founded by Sundiata Keita in the thirteenth century. Under rulers such as Mansa Musa it presided over one of the richest states of the medieval world.

kenjutsu.s: Kenjutsu is the Japanese art of swordsmanship. During the long peace of the Edo period, elaborate kenjutsu schools developed, emphasising technique, discipline and ritual.

kente-cloth.s: Kente cloth is a brightly coloured woven textile of the Akan peoples of present-day Ghana, made from interwoven strips of cloth. It was associated with royalty and important occasions.

kerma.s: Kerma is an archaeological site and ancient city in northern Sudan, the centre of a major Nubian kingdom from around 2500 BCE. It was the first centre of the Kushite state before power shifted to Napata and Meroë.

kerman.s: Kerman is a city in south-eastern Iran. In 1794 the last Zand ruler, Lotf Ali Khan, was captured there by Agha Muhammad Khan Qajar after a prolonged siege.

kertanegara.s: Kertanegara was the last king of Singhasari in eastern Java. Around c.

khabur-river.s: The Khabur River is a tributary of the Euphrates in north-eastern Syria. Its valley was the heartland of the Mitanni Empire and its capital Washukanni.

khagan.s: Khagan, also qaghan, was the title of the supreme ruler among the Turkic and Mongol peoples, meaning khan of khans. It was used by the rulers of the Gokturk Empire and the Khazar Khaganate.

khalid-ibn-al-walid.s: Khalid ibn al-Walid was an Arab military commander of the early Islamic period, celebrated as one of the most successful generals of his age. Leading armies for the Rashidun Caliphate, he played a central part in campaigns against the Sasanian Empire in Iraq and the Byzantine…

khalifa.s: Khalifa, rendered in English as caliph, is the Arabic title for the successor to the Prophet Muhammad as leader of the Muslim community. The office emerged after Muhammad's death in 632, when Abu Bakr became the first caliph of the Rashidun Caliphate.

khalsa.s: The Khalsa is the collective body of initiated Sikhs, established by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699 as a community bound by shared discipline, identity and readiness to defend the faith. It provided the ideological and military core from which the Sikh Empire emerged under Ranjit…

khalwa.s: Khalwa refers to the Quranic schools found across the Sudanic belt of Africa, where pupils learned to recite and write the Quran and received basic religious instruction. In the Wadai Empire, a network of khalwa schools provided literacy and Islamic education under the…

khami.s: Khami is an archaeological site in south-western Zimbabwe, known for its terraced dry-stone walls and enclosures. It belongs to the stone-building tradition descended from Great Zimbabwe and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

khanbaliq.s: Khanbaliq, meaning 'city of the khan', was the capital built by Kublai Khan on the site of present-day Beijing. It served as the principal seat of the Yuan Dynasty and was laid out on a planned grid with imperial palaces at its centre.

kharaj.s: Kharaj was a land tax levied in Islamic states on agricultural land, originally applied to territory conquered by Muslim armies and worked by non-Muslim cultivators. It formed a key source of revenue for the Rashidun and Umayyad Caliphates, where disputes over its payment by…

kharak-singh.s: Kharak Singh was the eldest son and successor of Ranjit Singh, founder of the Sikh Empire. His brief reign after his father's death in 1839 was dominated by court intrigue, and he died under suspicious circumstances in 1840.

kharijites.s: The Kharijites were an early Islamic sectarian movement that broke away from the caliph Ali after he agreed to arbitration with Muawiya at Siffin in 657. They held that leadership should be determined by piety rather than descent and rejected rulers they judged sinful.

khazar-khaganate.s: The Khazar Khaganate was a Turkic steppe state that controlled the region between the Black Sea, the Caspian and the Volga from the seventh to the tenth century. Emerging from the western fringes of the Gokturk world, it grew wealthy from trade between Europe, the Islamic…

khitans.s: The Khitans were a nomadic people of the Mongolian and Manchurian steppe who founded the Liao dynasty in northern China in the tenth century. Earlier they had been among the peoples subject to or neighbouring the Gokturk Empire.

khiva.s: Khiva is a city in the Khwarazm region of present-day Uzbekistan, long the capital of the Khanate of Khiva. Nader Shah of the Afsharid Empire campaigned against it in 1740 during his Central Asian expeditions.

khmelnytsky-uprising.s: The Khmelnytsky Uprising was a Cossack rebellion that began in 1648 under Bohdan Khmelnytsky in the Ukrainian lands of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Drawing on Cossack, peasant and Orthodox grievances against Polish magnates, it inflicted heavy defeats on Commonwealth…

khmer-empire.s: The Khmer Empire was a Hindu-Buddhist state centred on Angkor in present-day Cambodia, dominant in mainland South-East Asia from the ninth to the fifteenth century. It is known for monumental temple complexes such as Angkor Wat and for an elaborate system of reservoirs and…

khorasan.s: Khorasan is a historical region of north-eastern Iran and adjoining parts of Central Asia and Afghanistan, containing cities such as Nishapur, Merv and Herat. It was the launching ground of the Abbasid revolution against the Umayyad Caliphate and the base from which the…

khorsabad.s: Khorsabad is the modern name of the site of Dur-Sharrukin, the royal city built by the Assyrian king Sargon II in northern Iraq in the late eighth century BCE. Its palace was decorated with monumental reliefs and colossal winged bull figures.

khosrow-i.s: Khosrow I, also known as Anushirvan, was a Sasanian king who reigned in the sixth century CE and is remembered as one of the dynasty's greatest rulers. He reformed taxation and the army, strengthening central control over the Sasanian Empire.

khosrow-ii.s: Khosrow II was the last great king of the Sasanian Empire, reigning in the late sixth and early seventh centuries CE. His long war against the Byzantine Empire brought Sasanian armies to Egypt and Anatolia before a Byzantine counter-offensive reversed these gains.

khutba.s: The khutba is the sermon delivered at Friday congregational prayer in Islam, in which the name of the recognised ruler was traditionally proclaimed. Inclusion or omission of a ruler's name in the khutba was therefore a public sign of political allegiance.

khvarenah.s: Khvarenah, known in Middle Persian as xwarrah, is an Iranian concept of divine glory or royal fortune believed to accompany legitimate rulers. In the Sasanian Empire it formed part of the ideology of kingship, signalling that the monarch ruled with divine favour.

khwarazm.s: Khwarazm is a historical region around the lower Amu Darya river and its delta south of the Aral Sea, in present-day Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. An ancient centre of irrigated agriculture and trade, it gave its name to the Khwarazmian Empire, whose shahs built a large state…

khwarazmian-empire.s: The Khwarazmian Empire was a Persianate Muslim state ruled by the Khwarazm Shahs, which grew from the Khwarazm region into a major power in Central Asia and Iran around 1200. It displaced the Seljuks in much of the east.

khwarazmians.s: The Khwarazmians were the people and ruling dynasty of Khwarazm, whose shahs built the Khwarazmian Empire. They rose at the expense of the declining Seljuk Empire in the twelfth century.

khyber-pass.s: The Khyber Pass is a mountain pass linking Afghanistan with the plains of the north-western Indian subcontinent, in present-day Pakistan. It has long been a key route for armies and trade entering India.

kidinuid-dynasty.s: The Kidinuid dynasty was a ruling line of Elam that revived Elamite power around 1500 BCE. According to the Elamite Confederation profile, it introduced the unifying title King of Anshan and Susa, reasserting Elamite cultural identity after periods of Mesopotamian influence.

kiel.s: Kiel is a port city on the Baltic coast of northern Germany and was the principal base of the German Empire's navy. Its harbour and the Kiel Canal gave it strategic importance.

kiel-mutiny.s: The Kiel mutiny was a revolt by sailors of the German High Seas Fleet in 1918, sparked by orders for a final naval sortie against the British at the end of the First World War. The unrest spread rapidly to other cities, giving rise to workers' and soldiers' councils.

kievan-rus.s: Kievan Rus' was a medieval East Slavic state centred on Kyiv, flourishing from the late ninth to the thirteenth century. Its rulers attacked and helped destroy the Khazar Khaganate in the tenth century, removing a major power on the steppe.

kindattu.s: Kindattu was a king of the Shimashki dynasty of Elam. Around 2004 BCE he sacked Ur and captured the last ruler of the Third Dynasty of Ur, ending Mesopotamian hegemony over Elam.

king-of-anshan-and-susa.s: King of Anshan and Susa was a royal title of Elamite rulers, joining the names of the highland centre of Anshan and the lowland city of Susa. In the Sukkalmah period it formed one tier of a tripartite governing hierarchy.

king-of-bohemia.s: The King of Bohemia was the ruler of the Kingdom of Bohemia, a constituent realm of the Holy Roman Empire centred on Prague. Under the Golden Bull of 1356 the King of Bohemia was one of the seven prince-electors who chose the emperor.

king-of-the-lombards.s: King of the Lombards was the title of the rulers of the Lombard kingdom in Italy. After Charlemagne conquered the kingdom in 774, he assumed the title himself, adding Italy to the Frankish realm.

king-of-the-universe.s: King of the Universe, or King of the World, was a prestigious Mesopotamian royal title signifying universal rule. First used by Akkadian kings, it was later adopted by Assyrian rulers to express claims to supremacy over all lands.

kingdom-of-aragon.s: The Kingdom of Aragon was a Christian kingdom in north-eastern Iberia that took part in the Reconquista against the Almoravid and Almohad states of al-Andalus. Through union with Catalonia it built a Mediterranean presence.

kingdom-of-castile.s: The Kingdom of Castile was a Christian kingdom of central Iberia and the leading power of the Reconquista. It fought both the Almoravid Empire and the Almohad Caliphate, notably at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.

kingdom-of-dahomey.s: The Kingdom of Dahomey was a West African kingdom centred on Abomey in present-day Benin, known for its centralised monarchy and its role in the Atlantic slave trade. In the eighteenth century it was forced to pay tribute to the Oyo Empire after repeated Oyo cavalry invasions.

kingdom-of-great-britain.s: The Kingdom of Great Britain was the state created by the union of England and Scotland in 1707. It united the two realms under one parliament at Westminster and combined their commercial and colonial interests.

kingdom-of-hungary.s: The Kingdom of Hungary was a central European kingdom ruled by the Habsburgs from the sixteenth century onwards. Under the Compromise of 1867 it became an equal partner in the Dual Monarchy, governing its half of the state, known as Transleithania, with its own parliament.

kingdom-of-israel.s: The Kingdom of Israel was the northern Israelite kingdom of the Levant, with its capital at Samaria. It was conquered by the Assyrian Empire around 720 BCE, and much of its population was deported in line with Assyrian resettlement policy.

kingdom-of-italy.s: The Kingdom of Italy was the unified Italian state proclaimed in 1861 under the House of Savoy, lasting until the republic was established in 1946. It built the Italian Empire through colonies in Eritrea, Somalia and Libya and the invasion of Ethiopia.

kingdom-of-jerusalem.s: The Kingdom of Jerusalem was a Crusader state established in the Levant after the First Crusade captured Jerusalem in 1099. Its army was decisively defeated by Saladin, founder of the Ayyubid Empire, at the Battle of Hattin in 1187, after which Jerusalem itself fell.

kingdom-of-kanem.s: The Kingdom of Kanem was a state to the north-east of Lake Chad, ruled by the Sayfawa dynasty, which converted to Islam around the eleventh century. It controlled trans-Saharan trade routes towards North Africa.

kingdom-of-kongo.s: The Kingdom of Kongo was a Central African state centred on Mbanza Kongo in present-day northern Angola, flourishing from the fourteenth century. It entered into contact with Portugal in the 1480s, and its rulers adopted Christianity.

kingdom-of-macedon.s: The Kingdom of Macedon was an ancient Greek kingdom in the northern Balkans. Under Philip II it became the dominant power in Greece, and his son Alexander the Great used it as the base for conquering the Persian Empire.

kingdom-of-navarre.s: The Kingdom of Navarre was a small Christian kingdom in the western Pyrenees of northern Iberia. Its forces joined the Castilian and Aragonese armies that defeated the Almohad Caliphate at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.

kingdom-of-poland.s: The Kingdom of Poland, also known as the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland, was the Polish state that entered a union with the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. After a long personal union under the Jagiellonian dynasty, the two were joined by the Union of Lublin in 1569.

kingdom-of-portugal.s: The Kingdom of Portugal was a monarchy on the Atlantic coast of Iberia, formed during the Reconquista against the Almoravid and Almohad states. From the fifteenth century it launched voyages that built the Portuguese Empire across Africa, Asia and Brazil.

kingdom-of-prussia.s: The Kingdom of Prussia was a German state ruled by the Hohenzollern dynasty from 1701, known for its efficient bureaucracy and powerful army. It gained territory from Sweden and in the partitions of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, and rivalled Austria within the Holy Roman…

kingdom-of-sine.s: The Kingdom of Sine was a Serer kingdom in present-day Senegal, located in the region dominated by the Jolof Empire. It was among the polities associated with the Jolof confederation in its early period.

kingdom-of-the-lombards.s: The Kingdom of the Lombards was a Germanic kingdom established in Italy after the Lombard invasion of 568. Its pressure on the papacy led popes to seek Frankish protection, and Charlemagne conquered the kingdom in 774.

kingdom-of-the-netherlands.s: The Kingdom of the Netherlands is the Dutch monarchy established in 1815 after the Napoleonic Wars, succeeding the Dutch Republic. It governed the later phase of the Dutch Empire, including the Dutch East Indies, until decolonisation after the Second World War.

kingdom-of-upper-mesopotamia.s: The Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia was a state built by the Amorite ruler Shamshi-Adad I in northern Mesopotamia in the early second millennium BCE. It brought Ashur and other northern cities under one rule and is often treated as a precursor of Assyrian power.

kingdom-of-zimbabwe.s: The Kingdom of Zimbabwe was the state centred on Great Zimbabwe on the Zimbabwe plateau, which flourished from about the twelfth to the fifteenth century. Its stone enclosures and gold trade with the Swahili coast made it a major southern African power.

kish.s: Kish was an ancient Sumerian city in central Mesopotamia, associated in tradition with the first kingship after the flood. Sargon of Akkad rose to power from service at Kish before founding the Akkadian Empire.

kitab-al-farq.s: Kitab al-Farq, or Book of the Difference, is a political treatise by Usman dan Fodio, founder of the Sokoto Caliphate. It contrasts just Islamic government with the practices of the Hausa rulers he opposed.

kitbuqa.s: Kitbuqa was a Mongol general of Naiman origin who served under Hulagu, founder of the Ilkhanate. He commanded the Mongol forces left in Syria after Hulagu withdrew, and was defeated and killed by the Mamluks at the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260.

knighthood.s: Knighthood refers to the tradition of an elite class of mounted, heavily armed warriors bound by status and service to a ruler. The Sasanian Empire's profile notes that its armoured cavalry influenced Byzantine heavy cavalry and, through several channels of transmission, the…

kobbei.s: Kobbei was a commercial town in northern Darfur and an early capital or chief trading centre of the Darfur Sultanate. It stood at the southern end of the Darb el-Arba'in, the trans-Saharan caravan route linking Darfur to Asyut in Egypt.

koh-i-noor.s: The Koh-i-Noor, meaning 'Mountain of Light', is one of the most famous diamonds in the world, originating in India. Nader Shah of the Afsharid Empire carried it off from Delhi along with the Peacock Throne after his invasion of Mughal India in 1739.

koine-greek.s: Koine Greek was the common form of Greek that spread across the eastern Mediterranean and the Near East after the conquests of Alexander the Great. It served as the language of administration, commerce and culture in the Hellenistic kingdoms, including the Seleucid Empire.

kokand.s: Kokand is a city in the Fergana Valley of present-day Uzbekistan and was the capital of the Khanate of Kokand from the eighteenth century. The khanate was one of the Central Asian states conquered by the Russian Empire in the nineteenth century.

kola-nut.s: The kola nut is the caffeine-containing seed of the kola tree, native to the West African forest zone. It was chewed as a stimulant, used in social and ceremonial exchange, and widely traded northwards into the savannah and Sahel.

komnenian-dynasty.s: The Komnenian dynasty ruled the Byzantine Empire from 1081 to 1185, beginning with Alexios I Komnenos. Its emperors restored Byzantine military and political strength after the crises of the eleventh century, partly by relying on family networks and Western mercenaries.

konkan-coast.s: The Konkan coast is the strip of land along the western coast of India between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea. It was strategically important to the Maratha Empire, which built coastal forts and a navy there.

kontagora.s: Kontagora was an emirate and town in present-day north-western Nigeria, part of the Sokoto Caliphate. It was among the first emirates conquered by British forces under Frederick Lugard, falling in 1900.

konya.s: Konya is a city in central Anatolia, the ancient Iconium. It became the capital of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, the Anatolian branch of the Seljuk world, and flourished as a centre of trade, architecture and learning.

kopek.s: The kopek is a small unit of Russian currency, one hundredth of a rouble. Its name is usually traced to the spear (kopyo) carried by the mounted figure on Muscovite coins introduced in the 1530s.

kopje.s: A kopje is a small, isolated hill, often a rocky granite outcrop, rising from the surrounding plain in southern Africa. Such features are characteristic of the Zimbabwe plateau.

kora.s: The kora is a twenty-one-string harp-lute of the Mandinka and neighbouring peoples of West Africa, played above all by jali (griots), the hereditary musicians and keepers of oral history. Mandinka tradition places its origin in the Kaabu Empire, whose rulers and wars are…

kordofan.s: Kordofan is a region of present-day Sudan lying between Darfur and the Nile valley. It was a contested borderland over which the Darfur Sultanate and its eastern neighbours fought for control of trade and resources.

korea.s: Korea is the peninsula in north-east Asia between China and Japan, home to a succession of Korean kingdoms. It was deeply connected to Chinese dynasties, with the Han Dynasty establishing commanderies there, the Tang Dynasty intervening in its wars, and the Ming Empire…

kosciuszko-uprising.s: The Kosciuszko Uprising was a revolt led by Tadeusz Kosciuszko in 1794 against Russian and Prussian domination of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth following the Second Partition. Despite early successes, it was crushed by Russian and Prussian forces.

kosmoi.s: The kosmoi were the chief magistrates of the city-states of ancient Crete. Aristotle compared the constitution of Carthage with those of Sparta and Crete, drawing an analogy between Carthaginian institutions and the Spartan ephors and Cretan kosmoi.

kotoko-council.s: The Kotoko Council was the governing council of the Ashanti Empire, established at the empire's foundation around 1700. It brought together the paramount chiefs of the constituent Asante states, and its collective assent was required for major decisions such as war, treaties…

koumbi-saleh.s: Koumbi Saleh is an archaeological site in south-eastern Mauritania widely identified as the capital of the Ghana Empire. Arabic sources describe a twin city with a Muslim merchant quarter and a royal town.

kouroukan-fouga.s: The Kouroukan Fouga is the founding charter traditionally attributed to the assembly convened by Sundiata Keita after the creation of the Mali Empire in the thirteenth century. Preserved in oral tradition, it set out rules for the empire's social organisation, clan relations…

koutoubia-mosque.s: The Koutoubia Mosque is the principal mosque of Marrakesh, built under the Almohad Caliphate in the twelfth century. Its minaret is one of the finest examples of Almohad architecture and influenced later towers such as the Giralda of Seville and the Hassan Tower in Rabat.

koxinga.s: Koxinga, born Zheng Chenggong, was a seventeenth-century Ming loyalist commander who resisted the Qing conquest of China from bases on the south-eastern coast. In 1662 he expelled the Dutch East India Company from Taiwan after besieging Fort Zeelandia.

kubar.s: Kubar was a later capital of the Aksumite kingdom, to which the court relocated in the ninth century as Aksum declined. Its precise location remains uncertain.

kublai-khan.s: Kublai Khan was a grandson of Genghis Khan who became Great Khan of the Mongol Empire and founded the Yuan Dynasty in China. He completed the conquest of the Song Dynasty in 1279 and ruled from Khanbaliq.

kufa.s: Kufa was a garrison city founded by Arab Muslim forces in southern Iraq in the 630s during the Rashidun conquests. It became a major political and religious centre and served as the capital of the caliph Ali.

kul-tigin.s: Kul Tigin was a prince and military commander of the Second Turkic Khaganate, brother of the ruler Bilge Khagan. He died in 731, and his memorial inscription in the Orkhon valley is one of the earliest surviving texts in the Old Turkic language.

kulturkampf.s: The Kulturkampf was a political conflict in the 1870s between the government of Otto von Bismarck and the Catholic Church in the newly founded German Empire. Laws restricted the Church's role in education and appointments, reflecting suspicion of Catholic loyalties.

kumaradevi.s: Kumaradevi was a Licchavi princess who married Chandragupta I, regarded as the true founder of the Gupta Empire. The marriage brought the Guptas territory and prestige through alliance with the long-established Licchavi clan.

kumasi.s: Kumasi is a city in present-day Ghana and was the capital of the Ashanti Empire. It was the seat of the Asantehene and the Golden Stool, and the centre of the empire's government and trade.

kumwimbe-ngombe.s: Kumwimbe Ngombe was a ruler of the Luba Empire in Central Africa, whose reign is dated to about 1810 to 1840. He is counted among the kings of the empire's apogee, between Ilunga Sungu and Ilunga Kabale.

kumwimbe-tshimbu.s: Kumwimbe Tshimbu was a claimant to the Luba throne in the late nineteenth century. After the death of Ilunga Kabale, he fought a civil war against his rival Kasongo Nyembo.

kupechestvo.s: Kupechestvo was the merchant estate of the Russian Empire, the legally defined class of urban traders. Merchants were organised into guilds according to their declared capital and held particular rights and obligations.

kurdistan.s: Kurdistan is a mountainous region inhabited largely by Kurds, spanning parts of present-day Turkey, Iran, Iraq and Syria. It formed a frontier zone between the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire, and its control was repeatedly contested in their wars.

kurds.s: The Kurds are an Iranian-speaking people of the mountainous region of Kurdistan in the Middle East. The Ayyubid dynasty was of Kurdish origin, and Saladin, its founder, rose to power through service in Zengid armies.

kurgan.s: A kurgan is a burial mound raised over a grave, a form of tomb common across the Eurasian steppe from prehistoric times. Elite Xiongnu burials were placed in such mounds, and the Xiongnu Empire's profile notes that their contents, including Chinese bronzes, Bactrian gold work…

kurultai.s: A kurultai was a political and military assembly of Mongol and Turkic chiefs, convened to choose leaders and decide major matters. At the kurultai of 1206, Temujin was proclaimed Genghis Khan, marking the foundation of the Mongol Empire.

kuruva.s: Kuruva was a system of tribute and taxation used in the Zimbabwe plateau states. According to the Rozvi Empire's profile, the Rozvi inherited it from the Mutapa, requiring traders operating within the empire to pay tribute directly to the Changamire's court.

kushan-empire.s: The Kushan Empire was a state founded by the Yuezhi in Bactria that expanded into northern India in the first centuries CE. Its control of trade routes between China, India, Persia and the Roman world made it wealthy, and it patronised Buddhism and Gandharan art.

kushite-empire.s: The Kushite Empire, or Kingdom of Kush, was a Nubian state on the middle Nile in present-day Sudan, centred successively on Kerma, Napata and Meroe. Long under Egyptian New Kingdom rule, Kush later conquered Egypt and ruled it as the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty in the eighth and…

kutama-berbers.s: The Kutama were a Berber tribal confederation of the mountains of eastern Algeria. Converted by the Ismaili missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shii, they provided the military force that overthrew the Aghlabids and established the Fatimid Caliphate in 909.

kutik-inshushinak.s: Kutik-Inshushinak (also read Puzur-Inshushinak) was the last king of the Awan dynasty of Elam, ruling around 2100 BCE. After the collapse of Akkadian power he freed Susa, brought Anshan and much of the Iranian plateau under his rule and campaigned into northern Babylonia,…

kutir-nahhunte.s: Kutir-Nahhunte was a king of the Shutrukid dynasty of Elam, the son of Shutruk-Nahhunte. Around 1158 BCE father and son defeated the Kassite dynasty of Babylon, carrying off monuments such as the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin and the Code of Hammurabi to Susa.

kwame-nkrumah.s: Kwame Nkrumah was the leader of the Gold Coast's independence movement and the first prime minister and president of Ghana, which became independent in 1957. He chose the name Ghana in tribute to the medieval Ghana Empire, though the old empire lay far to the north-west.

kwantung-army.s: The Kwantung Army was a group of the Imperial Japanese Army stationed in north-east China from the early twentieth century. Its officers staged the Mukden Incident of 1931, which led to the occupation of Manchuria, and often acted independently of the government in Tokyo.

kyoto.s: Kyoto is a city in central Japan that served as the imperial capital for over a thousand years. During the Tokugawa Shogunate the emperor and court remained in Kyoto, while real political power lay with the shogun in Edo.
